panels.figure_caption: Sagittal CT The aorta (labeled in red) serves as the primary anatomic landmark and is visible as the large midline vessel anterior to the lumbar spine. The celiac trunk (labeled in blue) arises from the anterior aortic wall and demonstrates focal narrowing at its origin due to extrinsic compression by the median arcuate ligament. The hook sign (labeled in blue) refers to the characteristic downward deflection of the proximal celiac trunk at the site of maximal compression, produced by the low-lying fibrous arch of the median arcuate ligament crossing the vessel anteriorly. Red arrows identify the site of stenosis. Post-stenotic dilatation (labeled in blue) is visible distal to the point of compression and confirms the hemodynamic significance of the stenosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A is a CTA sagittal view demonstrating the hallmark compression of the celiac artery by the median arcuate ligament, fulfilling the criteria for MALS visualization. B: Panel B is an axial CTA showing complications (dissection/aneurysm) arising from the severe stenosis and compression characteristic of MALS. C: Panel C is a CTA coronal MIP image demonstrating collateral vessel formation, a common physiological response to chronic stenosis associated with MALS.

The hyperdense area seen on the non-contrast study corresponds to a non-enhancing area on CTA surrounding the celiac artery, most likely representing an intramural hematoma. C) Coronal maximum intensity projection (MIP) image demonstrates a collateral vessel (white arrow) between the celiac artery and the superior mesenteric artery. CTA: Computed tomography angiography.
in_text_mentions: A CTA of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained for further evaluation, which revealed the titular pathology of this case report. The scan showed a 1.3 cm dissecting aneurysm of the celiac axis with severe stenosis proximal to the aneurysm and evidence of compression by the median arcuate ligament of the diaphragm, as the celiac trunk coursed behind it. Additional findings included collateral circulation between the celiac axis and the superior mesenteric artery, suggestive of MALS (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: Laboratory investigations were within normal parameters initially. Contrast-enhanced CT angiography revealed a distinct focal narrowing at the proximal celiac trunk with a reduction in luminal diameter estimated at approximately 60% (Figure 1). Downstream reexpansion of the vessel was evident, consistent with extrinsic vascular compression. Collateral arterial flow was also observed, raising suspicion for chronic hemodynamic compromise. These findings were consistent with MALS [5,6].
